items.title: Designing a Shared Platform to Serve Competing Institutional Clients Without Cross-Contamination
items.author: Anil
items.content:
• In the SaaS multi-tenancy model, we assume tenants to be the same. When you have competition between tenants, and at the same time the platform operator is a player in the same market, we have a conflict of interest issue that is beyond that of simple access control. 
  •  We use RBAC, separate schemas per tenant, and network segmentation to prevent unauthorized access. This does nothing to stop the issue of an on-call engineer or an internal trading desk from being in a structural conflict of interest.
  • Split: we divide the platform into a truly tenant blind core, separate per-client extensions which are independent for each instance, and infrastructure which enforces isolation. This turns “whose code is running” from a runtime decision into at deployment time which is also auditable. 
  • We put isolation forward as a tiered versioned feature which we discuss in commercial terms instead of it being a silent assumption in the architecture.
  • In production, what we see are leaks from logs, dashboards, and caches, which are the layers teams put in last, not from the primary data store which gets the bulk of the design attention. 

The Problem With “Just Add RBAC”

A platform I have helped to build and run which puts out market and index data, that also hosts investment analysis and which provides trade execution connectivity. We use it internally to the company and also license it out to a dozen or so external institutional clients, some of which are direct competitors for the same order flow, and a few which compete in more narrow terms with what we are trying to do. That which we did not include is what makes the isolation issue different from the multi-tenant SaaS which is familiar to most of us and has played a role in almost every architectural decision we made over the past few years, which in turn has shaped this model.

Most multi-tenancy guidance—AWS’s SaaS Lens, Azure’s guidance on multitenant architecture, and a decade of Salesforce engineering writeups—starts from the idea that tenants are indifferent to one another. A retailer using a shared e-commerce platform generally does not care who else uses it. That premise fails in capital-markets infrastructure and in related settings: healthcare networks serving competing insurers, ad tech platforms serving competing brands, and any B2B platform whose vendor is also a market participant. Isolation in these contexts is not just a minor detail of customer experience but rather a key part of the contractual and reputational framework, since revealing the position details of the other client by one of the clients can lead to serious troubles for the company. One cache key revealing a competitor’s pricing input, or a support dashboard that lets an engineer view two clients’ order flow side by side, could end a contract or prompt a regulatory inquiry.

Although RBAC, per-tenant schemas, and network segmentation are important, they are not enough by themselves. They work to prevent unauthorized access; the more challenging problem comes when legitimate access causes a conflict of interest. An engineer investigating one client’s incident, for instance, should not end up seeing another client’s data simply because the underlying systems are shared. Nor should the operator’s own trading desks obtain an informational advantage from running the infrastructure through which other desks trade.

Where Isolation Actually Fails

Four failure modes recur, and none of them are solved by tightening access control.

Aggregate leakage that RBAC doesn't catch. Row-level security prevents unauthorized reads but not de-anonymization. We have a share which is to calculate “average order size of this instrument for today” that is technically anonymized until a counterparty that knows their own order size leaves out the details of others’ orders, which is easy in a thin market. It is the same statistical disclosure issue that NIST’s de-identification guidance reports for personal data but applied to market microstructure instead. The solution isn’t in better anonymization math; it is don’t build the cross-tenant aggregate in the first place until a specific client has opted into contributing to it.

Customization that leaks into the core. Under stress to deliver, an engineer puts in one client’s custom risk rule as an if client_id '.' in a shared service instead of through a proper interface. Over the next few months, we see the same thing with 3 more clients’ branches appear, the test matrix grows exponentially, and we release a bug in one client’s branch which affects service for a client that has no connection to that code path and which didn’t know their SLA had slipped. It isn’t that people set out to do it this way; it just grows one reasonable excuse at a time.

Operational access as an unmanaged trust boundary. Production support requires we have wide access, which is a low level of risk in most SaaS environments. What we find is that when these people are from the same markets as our customers, then we have a standing conflict of issue, a structural one at that, and also a security issue. An engineer who can see any customer’s data during an incident has that very same visibility as an insider trading professional may abuse, -- it doesn't matter if it isn’t a known issue. We do not account for this in standard incident response training because it is assumed the responder has no part in the result.

Shared infrastructure as a timing side channel. Even in the best of clean data isolation scenarios, we still see information escape via latency and ordering. If one client’s large order causes a short-term backup in a shared routing component which is used by all clients, at the same time another client gains some insight into market activity from that delay, the exact type of issue that was looked at in the cloud VM side channel studies. This is the issue which teams put off to last as there is no actual data breach in the classic sense; the information is passed through the delay in the system rather than in a data field.

Three Layers, Three Trust Levels

The fix is architectural, not procedural: Split out the platform into layers which present different and defined isolation postures as opposed to is for isolation being an implicit side effect of how the deployment happens to be wired. 

The core —  As for reference data ingestion, market data normalization, platform wide observability plumbing, we have designed them to be tenant blind. There is no ability for identity to branch at all; it is stripped at ingress and reattached only at egress.

We back this with a CI check, not just a code-review convention, because “just this once” branches have a half-life measured in years, not sprints:

# ci/tenant-isolation-check.yml
- name: Enforce tenant-blind core
    if grep -RIn "tenant_id\|client_id" src/core/ \
        | grep -v "// tenant-context-boundary"; then
      echo "FAIL: tenant identity referenced outside context boundary in core/"

It is a very black-and-white check, which is not foolproof by itself; a dedicated engineer can still get around a grep-based gate. What it does do is catch the common issue, the well-intended “just this once” branch, before it goes out the door, and also it doesn’t require a reviewer to notice. We use it in conjunction with a regular manual review of the extension boundary for that which is more premeditated.

The extension layer keeps client-specific logic—custom risk checks, bespoke report formats, and proprietary connectivity—behind a small set of versioned interfaces. Each client's extension operates in isolation and does not run in a shared library in a multi-tenant execution environment. Of the three layers that we deploy, this layer has the greatest effect on the profile of incidents we experienced. Consequently, it transforms “who runs which code” from a runtime question into a fact defined at deployment time, thus rendering the system more comprehensible and easily auditable. If an extension is slow and buggy for one client, it is not able to affect any other client as no pool of threads, processes, or nodes is shared between the two.

On the infrastructure side, isolation guarantees separation of the storage, secrets, and network paths of different tenants. This results, for example, in the use of different encryption keys, creation of separate network namespaces, and observability pipelines. The latter is especially important given that logs and traces usually have lower access controls than data that is actually in production, and this is where the leaks happen.

A governance artifact that can be helpful is an isolation tier that is declared and has a version for each tenant, which has been reviewed during onboarding as well as whenever there is an architecture change.

Tier 3 costs more because that client gives up most of the savings associated with a shared platform. This is intentional as well. The table gives a clearer illustration of the commercial trade-off instead of implicitly assuming that the standardized controls for the shared platform will fit every partnership.

What Broke, and What We'd Do Differently

Throughout the investigation of various high-profile cases, we have come across logs, dashboards, or support tools, while we have hardly come across the main data storage system that has been developed with a lot of attention with respect to its isolation features. We have noticed that in one of the cases a support panel was created that enabled an engineer to eliminate selected instrument data across all customers by default.of requiring a tenant scope first. The dashboard was operational for a number of months before an internal audit uncovered the issue. We have not found any evidence of the dashboard actually having been used to cross tenant boundaries, but there is a difference between “no evidence of misuse” and “structurally impossible.” This is what needs to be established in the current domain. We only noticed the issue after changing our approach to the control plane from just the data plane.

The CI gate blocking tenant-ID branches in core code was the mechanical control that paid off fastest. It was cheap to write, and it eliminated an entire class of “just this once” branches that had previously slipped through review. That alone is not enough, so we pair it with periodic manual audits. Still, as a first line of defense, it has worked better than asking reviewers to spot the pattern by eye. Cache-key discipline is another matter: easy to describe, surprisingly difficult to enforce. Caching is usually added by whoever is responding to a latency complaint, rather than by someone considering tenant boundaries. As a result, a key scoped only by instrument ID can quietly deliver one client’s entitled view to another. A shared, mandatory caching library with tenant scoping built in has held up better than any coding standard.

Migrating present shared branch logic into the extension model: we did so by running the old and new systems in parallel, which included a shadow traffic comparison for many release cycles and gradual roll out of the extension to users one at a time, which was slower than we had wanted but the only way to do it without at some point breaking user trust in the platform.

On launch of a new competitive client, we saw this as a good chance to reevaluate the existing isolation of our other clients. Also, we are seeing that new client agreements have more strict confidentiality terms as compared to what we had with earlier clients, which we boarded years ago, and it is easy to fall into the habit of going with the old assumptions rather than relook at them. We treated each new institutional client as a trigger to fully reverify the isolation model instead of just adding another tenant to it, and in that we found out a number of issues which were present before the current design.

RBAC is what we use for access control does what it is meant to do, but it doesn’t touch upon issues of conflict of interest and side channel risks, which are key in this field. A layered approach as a solution sits between the extremes of what we have, but it brings in its own set of complex issues, which we see in terms of deployment and on-board friction. There are more moving parts to put in play, and with governance adding a step to the process, we see client-specific changes take longer to get out than they would in a simple branch. With just a few tenants that are working together, that is overkill. The cost of this solution begins to make sense as you scale up the number of tenants and the competitive pressure increases, in particular when the operator is in the same space. What tips the balance is not so much the number of tenants but the increased competition, which is the real driver.

Our tools are used to promote a blind tenant core approach, while pushing client modifications via independent extensions. We also emphasize tiered guarantees in our work using a clear methodology. In addition, we see both observability and admin tooling as an integral part of the data plane rather than as an afterthought.

items.title: A Broken Map, a Bad Fix, and the Fallback That Was Doing Everything
items.author: 313toHND
items.content:
I run a small, free tool called USFoodInJapan, a map that lets Americans traveling in Japan search a hotel, landmark, or neighborhood and instantly see every nearby US fast food chain and convenience store (konbini), with distance and one-tap directions. No account, no app install, just a search bar and a map. It's a static site with no backend, no framework, just HTML, vanilla JS, and Leaflet.js for the map layer.

A few weeks ago, someone sent me a screenshot of the map with a giant "API KEY REQUIRED" watermark stamped across every tile. That kicked off a debugging story with a twist I didn't see coming: the fix I shipped first didn't just fail — it made the site worse. And the real cause turned out to be something that had been silently true for who knows how long before that.

The map used two tile layers: Esri's World Street Map as the "primary" source, with a handler falling back to CARTO's free raster basemap if Esri ever failed to load. Standard, boring, been running fine for months. Or so I thought.

CARTO had recently started requiring an API key for their raster tile endpoint and serving a watermarked placeholder image to unauthenticated requests instead of erroring outright — a real policy change, not a fluke. Since the watermark was showing up, my first assumption was: CARTO (the fallback) is degrading, so let's point the fallback somewhere else — plain OpenStreetMap tiles instead.

I shipped that. It made things . The map went from watermarked to completely blank.

/Diagnosis #2 (the real one)

That regression was the tell. If swapping the fallback broke things further, the fallback must have been doing more work than I thought. I went back to the actual Content-Security-Policy header in the site's file — and there it was: the directive had never whitelisted , Esri's tile domain, at all. Ever.

Which meant Esri — the tile source I'd built the site around, labeled as "primary" in the code — had likely been silently CSP-blocked in every browser since the day that header was written. Every real page load was hitting an instant and falling straight through to CARTO, which had been quietly doing 100% of the actual work despite being coded as a mere fallback. When CARTO's own free tier started requiring a key, both paths were effectively broken at once — and my first "fix" pointed the still-broken fallback chain at yet another domain that also wasn't in the CSP allowlist, so rendered.

The actual fix was almost anticlimactic: add the missing domains to . Two lines. But the lesson stuck — a fallback that's silently propping up your "primary" system for months is a landmine, because the day it also breaks, you lose visibility into two failures at once and end up debugging the wrong one first.

Turning the incident into an upgrade

While researching CARTO's raster changes, I found their own docs saying raster basemaps are being phased out in favor of vector tiles — sharper rendering, no @2x asset doubling, restylable at runtime. I liked the look of their vector "Voyager" style better than Esri's anyway, so instead of just patching the CSP and moving on, I migrated the whole tile layer to vector.

The tricky part: my map already had a working Leaflet setup: markers, popups, search, click-to-pin, and I didn't want to rewrite any of it just to swap tile rendering. JS renders vector tiles, but it's not a Leaflet plugin by default. The fix was , a thin compatibility layer that lets a MapLibre GL vector layer live inside an existing Leaflet map instance as . Every line of marker/search/popup code kept working untouched, only the base tile layer changed.

function addBaseLayer(targetMap) {
  const vector = L.maplibreGL({ style: CARTO_VECTOR_STYLE, attribution: CARTO_VECTOR_ATTR });
  vector.addTo(targetMap);
  vector.getMaplibreMap().on('error', () => {
    if (targetMap.hasLayer(vector)) targetMap.removeLayer(vector);
    L.tileLayer(ESRI_TILES, { attribution: ESRI_ATTR, maxZoom: 19 }).addTo(targetMap);
  });
  return vector;
}

This time, the fallback isn't hypothetical, it's wired to a real event and I actually tested it, by pointing the style URL at a nonexistent domain and confirming Esri raster genuinely takes over. Given how the original incident played out, I wasn't going to ship another "fallback" I hadn't proven works.

I also learned the CSP for vector tiles is a different directive than raster: only governs -tag loads, but MapLibre fetches vector tile/style/sprite/glyph data via , which falls under . And the style JSON I was pointing at () actually serves real tile data from a subdomain (tiles.basemaps.cartocdn.com). Easy to miss if you only whitelist the exact host you first tested against.

None of this was exotic. It was a one-line CSP gap that had been silently redirecting all real traffic through an undocumented fallback path for an unknown length of time, discovered only because an external service change happened to break the thing that was quietly propping everything up. If you maintain a fallback for anything, a tile layer, an API, a CDN, it's worth asking: do I actually know my primary path works right now, or do I just know the app renders?

USFoodInJapan is free to use if you want to see the vector map in action, or poke around for chains near wherever you're headed in Japan.

items.title: Securing a Smart Dog Collar: Secure Elements, Key Lifecycles, and Why TLS Isn't Enough on 5 Microamp
items.author: Vitaliy Gribko
items.content:
The key that was never really yours

Years ago I shipped a battery-powered NB-IoT pet collar and wrote about the firmware side of it: FreeRTOS, an STM32L4, safe OTA, and the small humiliations of making a radio live inside a dog's daily schedule. That article was about keeping the device alive. This one is about a question I started asking myself after the collar was already in the field, and it kept me up more than any battery budget ever did.

The collar authenticated to the backend the way most small devices do: a symmetric key, provisioned at manufacture, stored on the device, stored on the server. And one evening, while re-reading my own provisioning code, I noticed the shape of what I had built. The key sat in flash. Flash can be dumped. Debug interfaces are pins on the board unless you burn the fuses, and burning them makes field diagnostics impossible. The "secret" was a file on a chip that any motivated person could read with fifty euros of hardware and a weekend.

A key compiled - or flashed - into a device is not a key. It is a copy of a key, lying in the open, plus the hope that nobody looks. I had built a lock and hung the combination beside the door.

This article is the class of problems behind that evening, not the story of one collar: what actually breaks when you do cryptography in software on a microcontroller, what a secure element really is (it is smaller and more boring than the marketing suggests), why key lifecycle is the actual product, and how constrained protocols do authentication on a budget of microamps. Everything here stands on public specifications and public incidents. Your threat model may differ; the physics will not.

The threat model nobody puts in the quote

When people plan security for a small connected device, they plan for the network. TLS, certificates, maybe a VPN for the backend. When the device gets physically attacked, the standard answer is "nobody will bother with a $30 gadget."

That answer aged badly in October 2016. Mir, a botnet built mostly from IP cameras and DVRs - devices nobody bothered about - took a chunk of the internet's DNS offline for an afternoon [1]. Nobody attacked those cameras because the cameras were valuable. They attacked them because the keys were default and the shells were open. Your device does not need to be a target; it needs only to be available, and to be somebody's stepping stone.

For a battery-powered device, the honest threat list looks like this:

  •  The flash is readable. Keys inside firmware are keys with a deadline.
  •  One genuine device, dumped, becomes a hundred fake ones. The backend cannot tell them apart if the credential is the only identity.
  •  Capture a valid message today, send it again tomorrow. If nobody counts messages, the attack costs nothing.
  •  SWD and JTAG are wonderful for development and equally wonderful for attackers. Fusing them shut bricks your own field diagnostics.
  •  Timing and power traces leak secrets from naive software implementations. This is not theory; Kocher's  paper is from 1999, which makes it older than several of my colleagues.

None of this requires nation-states. It requires curiosity and a soldering iron.

The anthology of shame, all public record: Mirai built its army on default credentials shipped by the million [1]. Juniper's ScreenOS carried a hardcoded admin backdoor for years (CVE-2015-7755). Fortinet's FortiOS had its "magic password" (CVE-2016-1909). An RCE in a popular camera SDK, Devil's Ivy, swept whole product families at once (CVE-2017-9765) - one shared component, one key, one compromise per product line. Sony's PS3 signing key fell not to a backdoor but to a reused nonce: the "hardware-locked" key lived in software, and software repeated itself. LoRaWAN fleets have repeatedly been found joining with default application keys straight from the manual. There is a pattern and it is not subtle: a secret that is everywhere is a secret that is nowhere.

Why software crypto dies on a microcontroller

To be clear about terms: software crypto means the secret key lives in ordinary memory - flash or RAM - and the CPU runs AES or SHA on demand. It works beautifully right up until the moment someone holds the board.

  1.  A microcontroller has normal flash. Normal flash answers reads. If your code can fetch the key at boot, so can a programmer clipped to the bus.
  2.  Even with the key hidden, the algorithm runs on a CPU whose power draw is visible. DPA correlates those tiny current wiggles with key bits. Kocher demonstrated it against real DES hardware when "IoT" was not yet a word.
  3.  Manufacturing wants test access, support wants debug access, and shipping dates want both left enabled. Each enabled interface is a front door with a welcome mat.
  4.  Bake one symmetric key into every unit of a product line, and a single compromise becomes a thousand compromised units. There is no rotation because there is no channel to rotate over that does not already assume the key.

Every one of these has a public standard or a public paper behind it; none of this is secret knowledge. It is just knowledge that arrives after the board is spun, which is the worst possible order.

The secure element: a smart card wearing different clothes

The host path shown here ran on a real reader and a real card while writing this piece - ATR in, SELECT out, honest status words back.

The fix is older than the problem. A secure element is a smart card chip in a different package - the same technology that has lived inside bank cards and SIM cards for decades, evaluated against attack catalogs that include lasers, acid, and a microscope, and asked exactly one question: can it be made to output the key? The answer it is built to give is no.

What you get, concretely:

  • Key storage that refuses reads. The key is generated inside the chip or injected once during personalization, and there is no command that returns it. The host never sees its own key. Neither does your firmware dump.
  • Crypto that never leaves. The applet signs, verifies, derives - you send a challenge, you get a response. The secret participates without appearing.
  •  Entropy seeded and conditioned on-chip, because the analog noise of a secure element is a better source than the ADC of a microcontroller that also has to count a dog's steps.
  • A public, boring interface. APDU exchanges over ISO/IEC 7816-4: select an application, send a command, read two status bytes. The same protocol your bank card speaks at a terminal. On the host side, pcsc-lite - free, open source, twenty-plus years old - is all you need to talk to it.

The programming model on the chip is usually JavaCard: a small applet, isolated by the card's runtime, selected by an application identifier (AID). The GlobalPlatform specifications cover how applets and keys get installed, updated, and retired on the card. If you have ever written an applet for a SIM, you have already written firmware for a secure element.

And the host side is refreshingly small. Select the applet, exchange bytes:

$ python collar_select.py
ATR: 3B189657694C4C20200417
SELECT F000000001DEAD01 -> SW 6A82
follow-up INS 0x32 -> SW 6D00

That is the entire intimacy the host is allowed: eight bytes in, a MAC out, and the key stays inside a chip that was designed by paranoid people who assume lasers.

For the record: this exchange is not a mock-up. While writing this article, the snippet above was executed against a generic CCID reader and an ordinary wallet card. ATR in, SELECT out, SW 6A82 back - "applet not found," exactly as designed; a follow-up command answered 6D00, "INS not supported." A card without the applet answers every command honestly - with status words, never with secrets. That is the entire thesis of this article, demonstrated in ninety seconds on hardware cheaper than lunch.

And "assume lasers" is not a figure of speech. The attack catalogs behind secure element evaluations are public - they are the Common Criteria profiles - secure elements typically carry evaluations at EAL4+ or EAL5+ - and they read like a heist menu: simple and differential power analysis (watch the current, recover the key), electromagnetic emanation, voltage and clock glitching to make the chip skip the very instruction that checks your PIN, laser fault injection to flip individual bits, and microprobing: physically landing needles on the die. Against each of these the chip deploys countermeasures - randomized execution, dummy cycles, sensors that wipe state on anomaly. None of it is perfect; the game is cost asymmetry. A student can reproduce real DPA at home today with ChipWhisperer, an open-source side-channel platform that costs a few hundred dollars - which is exactly why shipping a bare software key in 2026 is not a risk decision, it is a gift.

Inside the applet: the other side of the conversation

The host snippet shows half the conversation. Here is the other half - read it for its shape, not as an install-and-run recipe: a JavaCard applet, written fresh for this article on the public API, that MACs the host's INS 0x32 challenge with a key that exists only inside the chip. Where that key's value comes from is the very next section's question:

Read both sides side by side and notice what is absent: the host code contains no key, and the applet code contains no key either - only a key object whose value arrives once, at personalization, through channels JavaCard isolates from the application. The secret exists in exactly one place on Earth, and no line of source code on either side of the conversation can print it. That is what "the key never leaves the chip" looks like when you spell it out in two languages.

One version note before anyone runs this.  needs Java Card 3.0.5 or newer, and most inexpensive developer cards still ship 2.2.2, where the call dies with a NO_SUCH_ALGORITHM exception - not because CMAC is exotic, but because the API you get depends on the card's runtime, not on your code. A card marked Java Card 3.0.5 Classic or newer (JCOP 4 and friends) understands this crypto suite as written; on an older card you would implement CMAC from plain AES primitives by hand - a fine exercise, and an early lesson in why the applet should treat the crypto suite as a parameter.

The wire between: hosting the element on an MCU

The reader in the demo above exists because a desk and a PC are the fastest pipe to a card. Remove the reader and nothing about the conversation changes: the same APDUs travel over a bare ISO 7816-3 link, and the microcontroller speaks that link natively. This is the hardware level of the next collar revision - and the honest headline is that the pipe is hardware, the conversation is software, and only the pipe is new.

 A smart-card-package element needs VCC, GND, RST, and I/O; CLK is optional, because many elements clock themselves from an internal oscillator, and when a part does expect an external clock, an MCU timer covers it. Two of those wires are not wires at all, they are policy. VCC comes from a switchable rail so the element can be power-gated between sessions. RST goes to a GPIO, which buys a subtle field capability: you can bounce the secure element without rebooting the firmware that is logging the incident. I/O is half-duplex, one line, open-collector by convention - the whole link is closer to a doorbell wire than to a bus.

The STM32 already speaks this dialect. The USART on an STM32L4 has a dedicated smartcard mode: half-duplex single-wire, 1.5 stop bits, a programmable guard time, and character timing derived from an ETU clock - the ISO 7816-3 framing, including parity-error signalling and the retransmission count, is hardware-assisted. T=0 character handling largely runs in silicon; T=1 block framing is a thin software layer on the same peripheral. What remains for firmware is small and boring, which is the compliment. In its shape, not a recipe - bit names live in the L4 reference manual:

Note the order in : configuration registers refuse writes while the peripheral is enabled, so the full smartcard setup - CR2, the guard-time and prescaler in GTPR, and the CR3 mode switch - is programmed while UE is still zero; CR1 turns the USART on last. That is the same order ST's own HAL uses for smartcard init.

A reset sequence, an ATR parse, an optional PPS negotiation to pick a faster bit rate, and that pump - a few hundred lines. No DMA glamour, no third-party stack required to say hello. The two  loops at the bottom are the whole art of working with data on a T=0 card: the chip either says 61xx "there is more, ask politely", 6Cxx "you guessed the length wrong, ask again with this Le", or answers with a status word that is never a secret.

, in order: power the rail, de-assert RST, catch the ATR (the element's self-introduction - parse the interface bytes, note the historical bytes), optionally negotiate a faster ETU with a PPS, then SELECT the applet AID and wait for 90 00. From that moment the firmware is a client: it posts eight-byte challenges and receives MACs. Every later session repeats only the last two steps - the ATR ceremony is for boots and glitches, not for every message.

 One task owns the element. Other tasks post sign-requests to a queue and sleep; APDU streams never interleave, because interleaving is how you get two partial commands and a very confused chip. The MCU's persistent state is counters and session handles - nothing key-shaped ever lands in MCU flash, which is the entire point wearing an RTOS hat. The one genuinely dangerous moment in the whole life of the device is a brown-out during personalization: cutting power while a key write is in flight is how a one-dollar chip becomes a paperweight. Hence a deactivation sequence before every power cut and a supply rail that sags slower than the element's write time.

 Between sessions the element is power-gated to its leakage floor; waking it costs one ATR ceremony, a few milliseconds, done rarely. Per-message cost is unchanged - symmetric MAC, microseconds of CPU - because the radio, not the cryptography, remains the only budget that matters. The collar keeps its single-digit microamps in sleep; the secure element sleeps deeper than the dog.

And the collar already carries one. The soldered eSIM on the tracker board is the same smart-card die in its smallest suit: an MFF2 package, five by six millimeters, hosting the carrier's applet, provisioned and rotated over the air by machinery the device never sees. The modem owns that link; the carrier owns the keys. That is the exact division of labor this article keeps arguing for - already shipped, working, on someone else's keys. The secure element adds a second die so that your keys, the ones your own backend depends on, live under the same discipline: born inside the chip, rotated over an authenticated channel, never readable by the device that uses them.

And to keep the receipts straight: the host conversation above was executed on real hardware; the MCU link described here is public-spec wiring - ISO 7816-3 timing from the standard, smartcard mode from the STM32L4 reference manual, pin budgets from the element datasheets - into which that proven conversation drops unchanged. A standard interface is a promise that this sentence can be written: the pipe is new, the bytes are not.

Here is the part that surprised me, and that I now believe is the actual difference between a demo and a product. The chip is the easy tenth.

A key has a life: it is generated, injected, used, rotated, and eventually revoked. Each stage has failure modes that have nothing to do with cryptography:

  •  Somewhere between the assembly line and your desk, the device receives an identity. If that step happens over an uncontrolled interface, your supply chain is your attack surface.
  •  The first conversation between the device and your backend establishes trust. Do it badly - a shared transport key, a default PIN - and every later secret inherits the weakness. For the applet above, this ceremony is literally where the key object receives its value ( over the personalization APDU) - and only after that does mac.init(key, Signature.MODE_SIGN) become legal on a physical card.
  •  Keys should expire. To replace one you need a channel that is already authenticated... by a key. This chicken-and-egg problem has exactly two solutions: a second, longer-lived key, or a hardware root that signs the transition.
  •  One device falls off a truck. Now the backend must reject its identity without bricking the fleet, and the fleet must learn about the rejection without trusting the rejected device to relay it.

None of these stages is visible in a demo. All of them are visible in year two of a deployment, usually at 2 a.m. When people say "secure element," this is what the phrase should call to mind: not a chip, but a pipeline that makes keys mortal and replaceable instead of immortal and exposed.

The public world solved this pattern repeatedly. SIM cards do it for billions of devices - over-the-air key updates are a routine, specified operation. Bank cards rotate keys as a lifestyle. The constrained-IoT world mostly still ships one symmetric key per device per lifetime and calls it a day. That gap is where the next Mir comes from.

The public cloud world has already industrialized the answer, and the patterns are documented openly. Claim-based, just-in-time provisioning: the device ships with a claim certificate, and its real identity is minted only at first boot, on the customer's network - AWS IoT documents this flow end to end. Azure Sphere did one better in spirit: a hardware root of trust feeding a security service that manages keys for the fleet's lifetime. Android's Verified Boot plus attestation is the same idea in your pocket: the chain from ROM to OS is measured, signed, and remotely provable. What these systems have in common is the direction of trust: the key does not exist before the device does, and nobody in the factory ever sees it in the clear. An IoT product of any size can copy this shape with one secure element per device and a backend that treats keys as inventory - born, rotated, retired - instead of constants compiled into a firmware image.

Authentication on a microamp budget

The collar sleeps at single-digit microamps. A full TLS handshake - certificates, asymmetric crypto, several round trips - keeps the radio and the CPU busy for seconds. On a battery meant to last years, seconds of radio are a budget line, and certificates are a size class the device cannot afford to store, parse, and verify. Public-key crypto is not free either: an ECDSA verification on a Cortex-M4 costs milliseconds-to-tens-of-milliseconds of full-tilt CPU, and in a device that measures its life in microamp-hours, that is a real entry in the ledger.

Constrained networks answered this years ago, and their answers are worth copying:

  •  derives per-session keys from a long-term application key at every join, then authenticates each frame with a message integrity code and up/down frame counters. No certificates on the wire, ever. The public specification is readable in an evening, and so are the public post-mortems of deployments that shipped default keys or reset their counters - a complete education, positive and negative.
  •  does object security for CoAP: each message carries its own integrity protection and a sequence number, with a replay window on the receiving side. No session handshake per exchange; the pattern assumes a pre-established context.
  •  exists precisely for the "we need an authenticated key exchange, in bytes, on a device this size" case - a compact AKE designed to run before OSCORE, orders of magnitude lighter than a TLS handshake.

The pattern underneath all three: one expensive handshake (or a factory-established key), then per-message integrity with counters and replay windows, in symmetric crypto, at a cost the battery can live with. If your protocol does not have frame counters and a replay window, it is not a constrained protocol; it is a wish.

Here is the whole pattern as a running toy - both sides, public primitives only, no custom cryptography, just composition. The master key stands in for what the secure element holds; the receiver keeps a replay window:

Run it and the third line prints the only verdict that matters: REJECTED: counter 41 already seen. That one line is the entire contribution of the replay window - and the reason a captured radio transcript is worthless.

One more budget line belongs here, because devices outlive deployments. A collar shipped today will sit on a shelf, then on a dog, for ten to fifteen years. "Harvest now, decrypt later" is not a slogan when the harvest window is measured in decades; anyone recording today's traffic is buying a lottery ticket on future compute. The public answer, ML-KEM (FIPS 203), exists - but lattice key exchange on a Cortex-M4 costs real milliseconds and real RAM, and on a coin cell that is a genuine engineering dilemma, documented painfully in the public papers on constrained PQC. The honest current posture for a device this thin: symmetric authentication done right, AES-class session protection, and a hardware root - so that when the asymmetric migration is affordable, it is a firmware conversation, not a recall. Suite-agnostic by construction, again, buys the future.

National suites are a fact of life

One more design property, cheap to get early and expensive to retrofit: the architecture should not care which cipher suites it runs. And "national suites" are not an exotic corner case - they are a standing fact of the industry. GOST, SM4, ARIA and SEED, Camellia: national cipher families from four different regulatory worlds, all with public English-language specifications and RFC coverage. If your device runs AES-GCM today and a regulator asks for one of these tomorrow, the request is not an attack on your architecture - it is a configuration change. If it is anything more than a configuration change, the architecture is the bug.

The GOST family makes a good public case study precisely because its paper trail is long and open. It starts with a Soviet-era block cipher, GOST 28147-89, declassified in the nineties and later carried into English-language RFCs. The modern standard, GOST R 34.12-2015, defines two ciphers in one document: Magma, the 64-bit-block successor of the old cipher, and Kuznyechik, a 128-bit-block design for the new era. Modes of operation live in GOST R 34.13-2015; the Streebog hash function in GOST R 34.11-2012. Every one of these has an English RFC you can read tonight: the cipher usages, the TLS suites, the hash - and, my favorite for this article's theme, a public RFC for re-keying: regular session-key renewal as a formalized protocol operation, exactly the lifecycle discipline the previous section keeps begging for.

The Kuznyechik story also carries the article's thesis in one anecdote. In 2019, an academic researcher published an analysis of its S-box and found a hidden mathematical structure - a compact algorithmic description of a table the standard presents as arbitrary constants [2]. Thirty years of standardization, and the true generator of the table surfaced not from the designers but from outside cryptanalysis. Whatever one believes about how that structure got there, the engineering lesson survives every interpretation: secret by design is fragile by design. A construction whose security story depends on undocumented choices will eventually meet someone who reads structure into the noise - which is, again, the argument for public primitives with public scrutiny, and against homebrew.

What concretely changes when a suite changes: block size (64 vs 128 bits changes how you pack counters and nonces), MAC construction and length, key sizes, and the performance profile on your MCU. Which is why the applet should accept the suite as a parameter, not as a personality - and why the backend ledger records it per device per epoch. When a migration request arrives, "suite-agnostic by construction" is the difference between a firmware update and a product recall.

The regulation is already here

If the engineering argument is not enough: the legal one arrived.  sets baseline security provisions for consumer IoT - no universal default passwords, a means to manage credentials, secure storage, secure updates - and it has stopped being a suggestion. The UK's Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure act has been in force since April 2024, banning default passwords on consumer connectables [3]. The EU followed harder: under the Radio Equipment Directive's delegated act, cybersecurity requirements for connected devices became mandatory from August 2025, with the EN 18031 series as the harmonized route [4]. The US Cyber Trust Mark is building the same pressure from the labeling side.

Read that list again and notice something: no universal default passwords, secure storage, updatable credentials. That is not a compliance document - that is the checklist below, wearing a lanyard. The eight questions at the end of this article stopped being hygiene advice somewhere in the last two years; they are now the shape of market access. A device that cannot answer them is not merely insecure. It is unsellable in a growing share of the map, and the share is growing.

Taped above my desk since the evening I re-read my own provisioning code. Eight questions before any device speaks to the internet:

  1. Where was the key born, and who else was in the room?
  2. Can the device output its own key? (The only correct answer is no, by hardware.)
  3. What authenticates the first message after power-on?
  4. Where do frame counters live, and what happens on reset or overflow?
  5. How does a key get replaced - over what channel, signed by whom?
  6. One device is stolen. Name the exact steps to revoke it and the maximum time the backend keeps trusting it.
  7. Which debug interfaces are open in the shipped firmware, and what does opening each one cost the attacker?
  8. What does the device do when the backend says "I no longer believe you"?

If any answer starts with "we should probably," that is a no.

The next hardware revision of the collar is already designed differently, and the difference is not a bigger microcontroller. It is a secure element beside the MCU, keys that have never touched firmware, message counters with a replay window, and a provisioning pipeline I would be comfortable demonstrating to a hostile audience - because the secrets involved are, by construction, not present anywhere I could accidentally show them.

The dog still does not care. The battery budget still comes first. But the collar is now a device whose keys can be revoked, rotated, and audited, and the door no longer has the combination hanging beside it.

The earlier chapter of this story - the firmware and OTA side - is . An independent teardown of the collar's firmware methods, published by WeSpeakIoT, is .

The lock is not the product. The lifecycle is.

  •  - the application protocol data unit: one command-reply exchange with the card, ending in two status bytes.
  •  - answer to reset: the card's self-introduction on power-up, including its name and preferred protocols.
  •  - application identifier: the address by which a host selects one applet among many on a card.
  •  - a tamper-resistant chip holding keys that cannot be commanded out.
  •  - the two classic smart card transmission protocols; T=0 is byte-oriented, T=1 block-oriented.
  •  - a subset-of-Java runtime for smart cards; applets are selected by AID and speak APDU.
  •  - the one-time injection of identity and keys into a device or card.
  •  - message integrity code: a MAC over (counter, payload) that makes tampering and replay visible.
  •  - a monotonic per-message number; the backbone of replay protection.
  •  - the receiver's bookkeeping of seen counters; below or inside it, messages die.
  •  - RFC 5869 key derivation: turning one long-term secret into per-purpose session keys.
  •  - a soldered smart-card package, 5 x 6 mm; the same die as a SIM or a bank card, dressed for a PCB.
  •  - the wallet-card form factor: 85.6 x 53.98 mm of plastic with a contact pad.
  •  - the public evaluation framework and its assurance levels; SE chips typically ship at EAL4+.

items.title: The Production Reality Check: Scaling SSE Subscriptions for GPU Orchestrators (Part 2)
items.author: Raja Chakraborty
items.content:
In my last post, we designed a dual Roaring Bitmap inventory engine that mapped our GPU rack runtime availability status to a tiny payload. We set up Server-Sent Events (SSE), tested it on localhost, watched the latency plummet to sub-millisecond levels, and felt like we had beaten the system.

Then, we released it to production.

By Tuesday afternoon, our bandwidth bill spiked. Our elegant bitmap architecture had crashed into the realities of network scale. Here is the story of how our network layer broke. How we redesigned our subscription routing to handle the load.

Our initial plan was simple: whenever a runtime's availability state changed on a GPU rack, serialize that rack's dual bitmaps and stream them to all active scheduling agents connected to that cluster zone via SSE.

At scale, the math caught up with us.

If a cluster zone has 10,000 active scheduling agents or edge nodes, and a runtime like Llama-3-70b runs out of free slots, we send a 100-byte payload to all 10,000 agents. That is 1MB. No big deal. But if we have 500 racks, and 10 runtimes change states every second under peak scheduler load, we are pushing:

10 updates/sec×10,000 agents×100 bytes×500 racks≈5 GB/s10 updates/sec×10,000 agents×100 bytes×500 racks≈5 GB/s

Most of those agents were executing static pipelines that didn’t even use the Llama-3 runtime. We were wasting CPU and bandwidth streaming updates no one cared about.

The Fix: In-Memory Watchlist Routing

We realized that scheduling agents only care about state changes for runtimes they are actively scheduling or monitoring.

Instead of broadcasting the entire bitmap, we built a  on our orchestrator gateway nodes. When an edge agent opens an SSE connection, they register a dynamic subscription of runtime IDs they are currently utilizing or targeting.

Edge Agent ---> Subscribe(Runtime: 10821, 44012) ---> SSE Connection Node

On the connection node, we maintain a thread-safe reverse index mapping runtime IDs to active agent sessions:

import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArraySet;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.mvc.method.annotation.SseEmitter;

public class RackSubscriptionManager {
    
    // Maps Runtime ID -> Set of active agent SSE emitters
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<Integer, Set<SseEmitter>> runtimeWatchlist = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public void watchRuntime(int runtimeId, SseEmitter emitter) {
        runtimeWatchlist.computeIfAbsent(runtimeId, k -> new CopyOnWriteArraySet<>()).add(emitter);
    }

    public void unwatchRuntime(int runtimeId, SseEmitter emitter) {
        Set<SseEmitter> emitters = runtimeWatchlist.get(runtimeId);
        if (emitters != null) {
            emitters.remove(emitter);
            if (emitters.isEmpty()) {
                runtimeWatchlist.remove(emitter);
            }
        }
    }

    /**
     * Pushes a lightweight delta update ONLY to interested agent nodes
     */
    public void notifyStateChange(int runtimeId, int bitmapIndex, String newState) {
        Set<SseEmitter> emitters = runtimeWatchlist.getOrDefault(runtimeId, Collections.emptySet());
        
        if (emitters.isEmpty()) return;

        // Tiny JSON payload instead of the entire bitmap
        String deltaPayload = String.format("{\"index\":%d, \"state\":\"%s\"}", bitmapIndex, newState);

        for (SseEmitter emitter : emitters) {
            try {
                emitter.send(SseEmitter.event().name("runtime-delta").data(deltaPayload));
            } catch (Exception e) {
                // Connection died, clean up
                emitters.remove(emitter);
            }
        }
    }
}

Now, when our backend detects that a runtime slot availability state changes (e.g., from Healthy to Low Availability), we only publish a tiny delta {"index":42, "state":"LOW_AVAILABILITY"} to the handful of edge agents who actually have execution chains dependent on index 42.

With this watchlist-driven subscription model, our network bandwidth dropped by  overnight. We were finally streaming data intelligently.

We celebrated. Our connections were stable, and our network egress was tiny.

But as any backend engineer knows, fixing one bottleneck simply exposes the next. As soon as our scheduling engines could see runtime availability in real-time, they started rushing to allocate the final remaining slots on candidate racks.

Our network layer was saved. But our database was about to seize up entirely from write contention and row locks.

In the next part, we'll talk about how we resolved DB hot-row locks during concurrent runtime allocations using a lock-free Redis reservation engine and append-only database ledgers.

items.title: Math Professor Accuses OpenAI of Copying His Work, Says AI Compute Power Makes Racing to Publish 'Pointless'
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
The New York Post wrote that OpenAI "stunned the mathematics world" last week when it announced its AI model "cracked a legendary math problem left unsolved for nearly a century in just 88 hours." 

But a New York University professor "has come forward alleging OpenAI may have copied his work after asking him to collaborate — with one of the company's scientists allegedly warning he might 'ruin his career' if he refused."


[P]rofessor Tristan Buckmaster, a British-Australian researcher who trained in Germany... had been working with Long Island-raised math prodigy Levent Alpöge, a researcher with OpenAI rival Anthropic, on a different elusive fluid dynamics equation, known as the Euler problem, when he found a solution using AI tools from both Anthropic and ChatGPT. He said scientists from OpenAI approached him and tried to convince him to jointly announce the solution, claiming they had independently solved Navier-Stokes. Buckmaster questioned the timing of their finding the solution in a blog post, noting OpenAI had only done so "in the past few days" — after the company became aware of his work. He asked OpenAI experts whether its AI systems used to solve the equation had been "trained on, or had access to" his research, but said they declined to answer, prompting him to wonder how they had advanced toward the solution so quickly. The puzzle is "not the direction one arrives at in a few days," Buckmaster wrote incredulously... 

 In OpenAI's post on its website sharing the Navier-Stokes proof, which it credited to Astra, the company's latest AI bot, the firm insisted no user data was incorporated into its model to solve the problem. However, it noted that it "cannot rule out" that anonymized data was used to "improve our models." 

"We congratulate Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster on their remarkable mathematical work," OpenAI said in the announcement. 

Buckmaster shot back, "Is it ethical to use customer's data to try to scoop their customer?" 

Alpöge's affiliation with Anthropic "seems to have been a sore point for OpenAI," writes TechCrunch.

Buckmaster's public statement says the OpenAI's Sebastien "twice asserted that he wanted Levent removed from authorship" and also said that "it was so annoying that Levent works at Anthropic" — but that Buckmaster still refused to remove the Anthropic mathematician's credit.

I said that if OpenAI released its result in the way proposed I would go
public with what happened. The reply was, "Why would you ruin your career?" [OpenAI's Bubeck said later on X that he'd meant unfounded accusations could damage Buckmaster's career.] I replied that I am an academic, and asked why he thought going public would ruin my career. The reply was, "If you don't want me to be nice, then I don't have to be nice."
 


Buckmaster later told Australia's public broadcaster ABC that the companies building AI "have zero respect for the scientific community. I mean, it's appalling, honestly." But he went on to say AI has made the race to publish mathematical breakthroughs pointless.

"I think it's pointless. Like, I think the game is up...." Professor Buckmaster said he and Dr Alpöge had more research they could publish but questioned the point of racing ahead with it when AI could perform work that had previously occupied researchers for years. 

He said there needed to be a discussion about how mathematics should operate in this new environment. Professor Buckmaster said some mathematicians had stopped publicly sharing what they were working on to avoid tipping off AI companies about their plans. He has called on academics and people from OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepMind to discuss ground rules for how they worked together.
 He said the companies' power carried responsibilities that went beyond competing to solve problems before their rivals... 

Building on the work of mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa, the pair found a solution to the Euler problem, a stepping stone to the Navier-Stokes problem. Professor Buckmaster said he spent weeks checking and improving the "slop" proofs generated by AI... 

For now, Professor Buckmaster said he wanted to finish existing work and support his PhD students and postdoctoral researchers, rather than chase another Millennium Prize. "I think it's more important to re-evaluate what math is," he said. 

"The New York University professor also warned Australia about the centralisation of resources into the hands of a small number of privately owned foreign companies..."

items.title: How to audit what your AI agents are accessing
items.author: ameliepangolin
items.content:
Have you ever asked an LLM in chat what seemed like a simple question, then watched as it reinvented fire, the wheel, and quantum physics to tell you how far Scotiabank Arena is from the Toronto airport?

AI agents, like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and OpenClaw, can do that, too. But their users explicitly encourage them to dig deep. Agents can make dozens of LLM requests per task, invoke tools, and pass data to one or more providers. So who sent what data to which model, and where is it logged?

If you’re using Aperture, you can see, store, and control access to this data.

Here’s how Aperture works to help you audit what your AI agents are accessing, who’s managing them, and where it’s all logged.

Every AI request has an identity attached

Aperture’s ability to rein in AI agent sprawl starts with its identity layer. Every request routed through Aperture comes with cryptographic proof of identity through Tailscale. When tokens are set on fire, you’ll know where the smoke started.

Every time a person or a agent makes a request through Aperture, their login name, device ID, and any related tags are pulled from their identity. The same goes for tagged “non-human” devices, like CI runners or background agents, which pick up an identity from their tags.

You don’t have to go message-by-message through a coding session or chat session, thanks to Aperture’s session tracking. Related requests are all grouped into sessions, so you can see the context of the data, tools, and costs associated with deeper work.

Identity flows through the whole system: every record, dashboard, and session log. You can always answer “Who did this,” and the answer is a specific person or device. Some vendors try to provide visibility by pulling every user, and every job, into a single ecosystem and control panel. Aperture provides consistent identity, visibility, and control layers across whatever tools teams choose to use.

What data is captured, where it’s kept

Aperture captures the full request-response lifecycle of every LLM interaction. Administrators get granular access and control to what data is being retained and where it ends up.

Here’s what Aperture captures:

  • The full request body from a user
  • Full response body from the LLM
  • HTTP headers (with sensitive values redacted)
  • Token counts by type (input/output/cached/reasoning)

All of this is captured asynchronously, after a response is completed. Aperture doesn’t slow down AI work in any way.

How much captured data you want to keep is up to you. You can reduce your capture log retention all the way down to zero. You can export logs to S3-compatible storage for your SIEM system so you can detect and respond to threats. Or you could do both, holding no data, but still having a full audit trail.

You can let trusted partners into your data, too. Aperture has already built APIs and integrations with Cribl, Oso, Apollo Research, and Cerbos, with more to come.

Who can see the logs (and who can’t)

Aperture’s access policy for session data is deny-by-default. Access to logs, just like access to models, is controlled through a grants system, one that can map directly onto Tailscale identities.

Grants can be highly specific (), categorical (), or open-door (). In Aperture, you can also scope by provider and model, like  or , and set MCP tool access through grants, too. There are two roles at the moment, user and admin, with more to come soon.

If you’ve already got Tailscale grants configured, you can set up Aperture in the same tailnet policy. Aperture and Tailscale grants combine additively.

Administrator access logging

Along with insights into AI use, Aperture, unlike most gateways, can also log what administrators do with those logs.

When someone with an admin role views logs owned by another user, the access is recorded. Other administrators can review the audit trail, either by API endpoint or Aperture’s web interface. It’s a clear signal to auditors that admin access to sensitive session data is both tracked and reviewable.

Enforcing policy before data leaves your network

Aperture’s policies wouldn’t mean much if all you could do is see what went out the door. By providing LLM access through Aperture, policies can be enforced  requests hit their providers, through guardrails. You can see not only what did happen, but what was blocked from happening.

  • Pre-request hooks can scrub personally identifiable information (PII), block requests that violate data policy, or strip out specific tool declarations
  • Should the guardrail service be unreachable, requests can be configured to fail_closed (blocked) or fail_open (proceed)
  • Aperture partners can add fine-grained authorization at the tool-call level, allowing or denying individual calls
  • Quotas can enforce spending per user, group, agent, or run, across all providers.

Auditing highly active AI agents requires identity, logging, and visibility into who can see what. Smart limits on data, tools, and spending are a natural outgrowth of Aperture’s gateway design. It’s a single place to see what’s happening, what happened, and what's being blocked from happening with your LLM tools.
